web_review.quote: For the purposes of deciding an application under clauses (a) and (d) of Order VII Rule 11 of the Code, the averments in the plaint are the germane; the pleas taken by the defendant in the written statement would be wholly irrelevant at that stage.
web_review.reason: The rule faithfully translates the judgment's Order VII Rule 11(a)/(d) screening method. The trust's recorded challenge and the identified plaint are appropriate procedural premises. Their ALL connective establishes the context in which the screening method applies, without establishing that the challenge succeeds. The conclusion correctly requires meaningful consideration of the plaint as a whole, distinguishes material factual averments from requested reliefs, and excludes the defendant's factual rebuttal from the initial screening assessment. The conclusion does not improperly establish that this particular plaint discloses a sufficient cause of action. The scope limits appropriately preserve rejection where a meaningful reading reveals an illusory or manifestly vexatious cause of action, and distinguish rejection of the entire plaint from striking out particular pleading matter under Order VI Rule 16. The judgment additionally emphasizes that omission of a necessary material fact can leave a cause of action incomplete, that a statutory bar must appear from the plaint for clause (d), and that Rule 11 imposes a duty to reject where its conditions are satisfied. These considerations are compatible with the rule's screening framework and its identified unimplemented semantic evaluation. NOT_COVERED is an appropriate burden policy because the supplied judgment does not establish a comprehensive evidentiary burden allocation for this reconstruction.

web_review.quote: The nature of the dispute is to be resolved by the Civil Court. The question of tenancy cannot be decided under Section 50 of the Act.
web_review.reason: The conclusion is faithful to the Supreme Court's characterization of the substantive controversy as the continuance, terms, and period of the tenancy, rather than an inquiry into the administration of the public trust. The rule appropriately consumes R1's screening framework and the target court's recorded characterization of the dispute. Its OPEN_TEXT connective is justified because determining the true substantive subject of a plaint requires interpretation of its material allegations and cannot be reduced to detecting tenancy terminology. The conclusion establishes civil adjudicability of the tenancy subject, not the existence of an eleven-year lease, the invalidity of an eleven-month lease, or the plaintiffs' ultimate entitlement to relief. The rule also correctly preserves the judgment's distinction between a trust tenant and a person having an interest in the trust for Section 51 purposes. Its scope does not generalize the Supreme Court's analysis into a complete determination of every Section 80 jurisdictional objection or the separate contention concerning the District Court's exclusive jurisdiction. Those limitations are important because the trial court and appellate courts had accepted jurisdictional objections, while the Supreme Court expressly declined to decide the separate District Court objection. No unsupported evidentiary burden is assigned.

web_review.quote: Such enquiries can only be undertaken under Section 50 of the Act. For instituting the suit of the nature specified in Section 50, prior consent of the Charity Commissioner is necessary under Section 51.
web_review.reason: The rule accurately preserves the distinct statutory treatment of the plaint's request to direct an inquiry into alleged illegal acts involving the trust and its trustees. Its single recorded-prayer premise establishes that the particular relief was requested, without establishing misconduct. The ALL connective is acceptable for this narrowly identified prayer; it does not purport to classify every conceivable trust-related relief automatically. The conclusion is supported by the judgment's express treatment of inquiries into trust affairs under Section 50 and its description of prior consent under Section 51 for suits of the nature specified in Section 50. Importantly, the rule does not convert those provisions into a general prohibition against civil tenancy litigation involving a trust. Its limitations correctly distinguish the Commissioner from the trust and trustees, acknowledge that the inquiry transaction is separate from the tenancy transaction, and avoid inferring either the presence or the absence of statutory consent without supporting evidence. The necessary case-specific assessment of differently formulated reliefs is expressly unimplemented. The judgment supplies no additional burden allocation requiring incorporation.

web_review.quote: Whether part of the relief cannot be granted by the Civil Court is a different matter from saying that because of a combined claim of reliefs the jurisdiction is ousted or no cause of action is disclosed.
web_review.reason: This rule faithfully translates the judgment's distinction between a defective cause of action and a plaint combining reliefs subject to different legal regimes. Its three premises appropriately connect the whole-plaint screening method, the civil-adjudicable tenancy controversy, and the separate trust-affairs inquiry route. The ALL connective is suitable for the narrow mixed-relief configuration addressed here. The conclusion is carefully limited to the proposition that combining those reliefs is not, by itself, sufficient to justify rejection of the entire plaint. It does not assert that every residual tenancy cause is adequate, that every claimed relief can be granted, or that Rule 11 permits partial rejection. The scope correctly distinguishes Order VII Rule 11 from Order VI Rule 16 and recognizes the separate procedural treatment of relinquished claims under Order II Rules 1 and 2. It also preserves the need for an appropriate trial-court application where relinquishment is sought, without treating the contemplated application as already made or granted. The Supreme Court's restriction of adjudication to tenancy, its terms, and its period is consistent with this narrow non-entailment rule. Independent reasons for rejecting a plaint remain subject to meaningful appraisal, as the unimplemented limitations acknowledge. The burden policy does not introduce unsupported requirements.

web_review.quote: This plea is strongly disputed by learned counsel for the respondent-trust who says that the possession was taken in accordance with law and as noted above, by voluntary surrendering by most of the tenants.
web_review.reason: The rule accurately reconstructs the presence of competing litigant assertions without deciding the underlying dispossession question. The plaintiffs' allegation of forcible eviction notwithstanding claimed continuing tenancy and the trust's contrary account of lawful possession-taking are expressly reported in the judgment. The ALL connective is suitable because the conclusion concerns the recorded coexistence of those opposing versions. The proposition established is that the assertions were advanced, not that either account is true. The rule properly avoids attributing voluntary surrender to the identified plaintiffs merely because trust counsel referred to surrender by most tenants or to 22 out of 44 tenants. Those reported descriptions do not independently identify the tenants involved, and the judgment does not establish the alleged surrenders through primary evidence. The rule also preserves the unresolved controversy concerning the duration of the trial court injunction and its possible significance for possession. It does not treat the Supreme Court's account of counsel submissions as independent documentary or testimonial proof. The evidentiary question remains unresolved, and the NOT_COVERED burden policy is appropriate.

web_review.quote: The question of forcible possession as claimed is also a matter which can be pressed into service by the parties before the trial Court and if raised the Court shall deal with it considering its relevance to the suit and accept it or otherwise reject the plea in accordance with law. We do not think it necessary to express any opinion in that regard.
web_review.reason: The central legal distinction is supported: survival of the tenancy controversy through plaint-rejection review does not itself prove forcible dispossession, establish a right to recover possession under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, or establish entitlement to a discretionary injunction. The judgment separately describes protection of settled possession against dispossession otherwise than by due process and the limitation on injunctions sought by persons in unlawful possession against true owners. It does not decide that either description applies to these plaintiffs. The rule also correctly identifies the importance of possession evidence, the opposing accounts, and injunction discretion. However, its premise structure and conclusion strength require correction before acceptance. The OPEN_TEXT rule makes specific UNKNOWN and CONFLICTED evidentiary states mandatory inputs to a non-entailment proposition that does not logically depend on those states. Procedural continuation would not itself establish the possession or injunction merits even if those issues were later established through independent evidence. Conversely, conflicting accounts are not necessary for the procedural-versus-merits distinction to apply. The predicate INJUNCTION_EQUITABLE_ENTITLEMENT_ADJUDICATED also requires careful separation of an expressly absent Supreme Court merits determination from uncertainty about the underlying entitlement or possible earlier interlocutory determinations. More importantly, the conclusion's statement that relevant evidence and discretionary injunction standards must be assessed in trial proceedings risks imposing a broader mandatory merits determination than the judgment directs. The Supreme Court restricted adjudication in the continuing suit to tenancy, its terms, and its period. It permitted the forcible-possession plea to be raised and considered only if raised and relevant to that suit, and expressed no opinion on its merits. The judgment did not independently order adjudication of an injunction entitlement claim. The rule's scope limits partially recognize these qualifications but do not cure the stronger operative wording or unnecessary status-dependent premises. The discretionary injunction evaluation appropriately remains OPEN_TEXT, and no additional evidentiary burden can be supplied from the judgment.
exceptions_or_scope_missing: The operative conclusion must preserve the judgment's qualification that a forcible-possession contention is considered by the trial court only if raised and relevant to the continuing suit.

The operative conclusion must respect the express restriction of continuing adjudication to the tenancy, its terms, and its period; it must not independently mandate a trial determination of injunction entitlement.

The non-entailment of possession and injunction merits from procedural continuation must not depend on settled possession being UNKNOWN, unlawful dispossession being CONFLICTED, or injunction adjudication being UNKNOWN.

The absence of a Supreme Court merits determination must remain distinct from the truth or falsity of the underlying entitlement, and from any incompletely described interlocutory injunction proceedings.
Any eventual Section 6 assessment requires its own applicable possession, consent, and due-process evaluation; it must not be collapsed into discretionary injunction analysis.

The judgment identifies prima facie case, balance of convenience, unlawful possession against a true owner, and judicial discretion as relevant considerations, but does not establish that these factors form an exhaustive conjunctive checklist.
